terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to call your functions with a few orders.

tasks.title: Write the candle label
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/functions.js`, give `candleLabel` two parameters, `scent` and `grams`, in that order, and make it return a label like `Cedar candle, 200 g`.

Check calls `candleLabel` with other scents and sizes and compares the text it gives back.
nextSteps: Name the two parameters between the round brackets after `candleLabel`.
Build the label from them inside the curly braces.
Run `node src/functions.js`: the first line should now be a label.
hints: A function only knows the values it is given. Parameters are the names those values get inside it.
Printing is not giving back. `console.log` shows text in the terminal; `return` hands a value to whoever called the function.
The function has the shape `function candleLabel(scent, grams) { return ... }`, where the dots are a template literal built from the two names.

tasks.title: Shipping for any order
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, first write a function of your own called `zonePrice`, from the word `function` to its closing brace. It has one parameter, `zone`, and returns the shipping for that zone in cents: `250` for `'local'`, `495` for `'national'` and `1295` for anywhere else. It only helps `shippingFor`, so it stays off the `export` line.

Then give `shippingFor` two parameters, `totalCents` and `zone`. It returns `0` when `totalCents` is 5000 or more, wherever it goes, and otherwise what `zonePrice` gives for the zone.

Check calls `zonePrice` and `shippingFor` with big and small orders in every zone, and reads your file for `zonePrice` and the call to it inside `shippingFor`.
nextSteps: Above `shippingFor`, write `function zonePrice(zone) {` and its closing `}` yourself.
Inside it, return the price for each zone, ending with the price for anywhere else.
Give `shippingFor` its two parameters, ask about the total first, and otherwise return what `zonePrice` gives.
Run the file and try a big local order and a small one abroad.
hints: A function of your own is written like the others: the word `function`, a name, the parameters in round brackets and the code in curly braces. Code in the same file can call it without the `export` line.
`return` ends a function at once, so each part of an `if` in `zonePrice` can give back its own price. Then `shippingFor` only asks about the total itself.
`zonePrice` starts `function zonePrice(zone) { if (zone === 'local') { return 250 } ...`, and `shippingFor` ends with `return zonePrice(zone)` after its question about the total.

tasks.title: Price with a default quantity
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, give `priceFor` two parameters, `priceCents` and `quantity`, and make it return `priceCents` times `quantity`. When `priceFor` is called without a quantity, it counts one candle. A quantity of `0` still costs nothing.

Check calls `priceFor` with and without a quantity, and with 0.
nextSteps: Name the two parameters and return the product.
Call `priceFor(1250)` and look at what comes back.
Give `quantity` a default value, as the lesson shows.
Run the file again: both lines for Task 3 should be prices.
hints: A parameter that is left out when the function is called is `undefined`, and a number times `undefined` is `NaN`.
A parameter can have a default value, written right where it is named. It is used only when that value is left out.
The first line has the shape `function priceFor(priceCents, quantity = ...) {`, with the default quantity after the `=`.

tasks.title: Put the order together
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, give `orderTotal` three parameters, `priceCents`, `quantity` and `zone`, and make it return what the customer pays: the price of the candles plus the shipping for that price. Call `priceFor` and `shippingFor` inside it instead of writing their rules again.

Check first makes sure Tasks 2 and 3 work, then calls `orderTotal` with several orders and looks for both calls inside it.
nextSteps: Inside `orderTotal`, call `priceFor` and keep its answer in a `const`.
Call `shippingFor` with that price and the zone.
Return the sum, and run the file.
hints: A function can call other functions. Their answers come back where you called them, like any value.
Shipping depends on the price of all the candles together, so `shippingFor` needs the price `priceFor` gives, not the price of one candle.
The body has the shape `const subtotal = priceFor(priceCents, quantity)` and then `return subtotal + shippingFor(subtotal, zone)`.
